newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-AWB Report-Frosts help Australian wheat crop.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-AWB Report-Frosts help Australian wheat crop.

text.p: Big frosts along Australia's eastern seaboard would do more good than harm, slowing up the crop and forcing it to tiller, the Australian Wheat Board (AWB) said in its weekly grain market report.
Some crops in the far northwest of New South Wales (NSW) and on the Liverpool plains were coming to a head, it said.
Crop conditions continue to be good for the most part in Victoria but some South Australian (SA) crops were in trouble, running to head on a single tiller, it said.
In southern NSW some black leg was showing up in canola but not enough to have a serious impact on yield. Elsewhere, pulses were handling the wet conditions well, it said.
There was little movement in the milling wheat market last week but some interest in feed grains.
Feed barley prices firmed in Queensland and northern NSW while remaining steady in other centres. New crop sorghum prices followed this trend rising by A$3.00 a tonne, AWB said.
Bids for winter wheat in Victoria fell by A$5.00 a tonne.
Canola continues its roller-coaster dropping back below the A$400 mark to A$392 a tonne delivered Melbourne.
Pulses were generally firm in all states although the bid for chick peas softened in SA.
The AWB's wheat indicator price closed the week at A$169.75 a tonne delivered Newcastle, down A$3 a tonne.
The AWB's indicator price for durum closed at A$220 a tonne Newcastle, a fall of A$1 for the week.
The AWB's estimate of the 1996/97 crop remains steady at 17.6 million tonnes.

Internationally, the AWB pointed out that the market opened strongly last week on the unlikely prospect of early frosts in Canada, while the presence of vomitoxin disease in soft red winter wheat may be an issue.
Egypt bought 150,000 tonnes of U.S. western white at the equivalent of A$238 a tonne during the week, it said.
